Disdain

/dis-DAYN/ — rhymes with rain · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Disdain is a feeling of strong contempt or scorn toward someone or something you consider beneath you.

She looked at the messy desk with obvious disdain.

Worked Example

The wealthy collector glanced at the counterfeit painting with obvious disdain, waving it away without inspecting it closely.

Disdain captures not just disapproval or dislike, but the sense that the painting is beneath the collector's attention and status. The collector doesn't merely dislike it; she considers it unworthy of respect — that mix of contempt and superiority is what disdain names.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

disrespect: rude treatment that ignores someone's worth

arrogance: an inflated belief in your own superiority

condescension: talking down to people you consider inferior

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

respect: sincere regard for someone's worth

admiration: warm approval of someone you look up to

Where it sits · how strongly you look down on it — dislike → disapproval → contempt → disdain

dislike vs. disdain: Dislike is much weaker than disdain; you can dislike a food or a song without believing it is beneath you.

disapproval vs. disdain: Disapproval is weaker than disdain because it only judges something as wrong, while disdain looks down on it as unworthy of your attention.

contempt vs. disdain: Contempt comes very close, but disdain is a notch stronger, adding a haughty, superior air of refusing even to consider the thing at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: do the opposite of; not (Old French des-)

Root — dain

Root — dain: to treat as worthy — from Latin dignari 'to deem worthy,' from dignus 'worthy'; the same root seen in deign and dignity (Latin (via Old French deignier))

Put it together

Put it together: The prefix dis- means 'the opposite of,' and the root dain comes from Latin dignari, 'to consider worthy' — the same root as in the English word deign. Put together, disdain literally means to treat someone or something as the opposite of worthy — to look down on it with contempt because you believe it is beneath you.

Use the root in a new word: dignity

Use the root in a new word: dignity: The judge treated every witness with dignity, making it clear she considered each person worthy of her full attention and courtesy.

Word Choice

formal / literary

Disdain is a refined, somewhat dramatic word for a very specific kind of contempt — one that comes from feeling superior. Use it when you want to show that someone looks down on something as beneath them, not just that they dislike it. For mild disapproval, 'disapproval' works better; for pure contempt without the superiority angle, 'contempt' alone works.
